paragraphs.heading: Who lives in the soil
paragraphs.text: Soil microbiology studies the microorganisms living in soil, what they do, and how they shape the soil's properties. Soil microbes fall into several groups: bacteria (among them cyanobacteria and actinomycetes), archaea, fungi, algae, protozoa and slime molds. Bacteria and archaea are prokaryotes and, apart from viruses, the smallest organisms in soil. They are also the most plentiful microbes there.

paragraphs.heading: Where it all began
paragraphs.text: Somewhere between two and four billion years ago, the first cyanobacteria, also called blue-green algae, appeared in Earth's oceans. They fixed carbon through photosynthesis and also fixed nitrogen. As they multiplied, they released oxygen into the air and nitrogen into the soil. That led to more advanced microorganisms, which mattered because they affected soil structure and fertility.

paragraphs.heading: Crowds around the roots
paragraphs.text: Microbes crowd around plant roots, in a zone called the rhizosphere, where each gram of soil can hold up to 10 billion bacterial cells that can be cultured. In 2011 one team counted over 33,000 species of bacteria and archaea on the roots of sugar beets. Away from roots, most bacteria in the bulk soil rest in colonies wrapped in a polysaccharide matrix and coated with clay, a state that withstands drought. They can stay at rest for a long time, until fluid from a growing root tip or the mucus of a burrowing earthworm reaches them.

paragraphs.heading: Feeding the soil with nitrogen
paragraphs.text: Nitrogen is often the nutrient in shortest supply in soil and water. Bacteria carry out nitrogen fixation, turning nitrogen gas from the air into compounds such as ammonia that plants can use. Bacteria also break down organic matter and help form soil aggregates, which improves the soil's overall health, and some colonize minerals and help weather them. Little is yet known about soil archaea, though they may matter a great deal for nitrification and methanogenesis.

paragraphs.heading: Versatile bacteria and antibiotics
paragraphs.text: Bacteria are chemically versatile. Pseudomonas can break down a wide range of chemicals and fertilizers, while Nitrobacter can only get its energy by oxidizing nitrite to nitrate. Actinomycetes are bacteria, yet many resemble fungi in shape, branching, spore formation and the making of secondary metabolites. One of their most notable traits is producing antibiotics, including streptomycin, neomycin, erythromycin and tetracycline.

paragraphs.heading: The work of fungi
paragraphs.text: Bacteria may outnumber fungi in cell counts, but in some soils fungi make up more biomass and respire faster. Fungi decay plant debris, especially wood, help bind soil into aggregates and serve as food for larger soil organisms. Some are soil-borne pathogens, while others, such as mycorrhizae, are helpful plant partners. The amount and quality of organic matter in a soil is directly linked to which fungi live there, and fungi do comparatively better than bacteria in acidic soils.
